title: DEBATE: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Evaluating Opinion Dynamics in Role-Playing LLM Agents
claim: Participants move through a timed sequence of private opinion reports and rounds of public posts and dyadic chats, tracing opinion change.
layout: Single wide timeline, left-to-right, with four participant swim-lanes and per-round partner changes
description: A wide, boxed figure titled 'Multi-Player Experiment', with a gray banner giving the discussion topic ('Everything that happens can eventually be explained by science.'). A gray timeline arrow runs left to right through labeled phases: Initial Private Opinion (2 mins), Round 1 Discussion (write tweets 2 mins, dyadic conversation 4 mins), Rounds 2 and 3 with the same structure, and Final Private Opinion (2 mins). Four participants appear as avatar rows, each with a color-coded arrow (blue, orange, green, purple). Speech bubbles on the arrows show tweets, responses and chat messages. Colored outlined boxes at the left and right edges hold each participant's initial and final opinion text. Below each box is a Likert scale (Certainly Disagree to Certainly Agree) with a dot marking the rating. Dashed vertical lines separate the phases. Partner colors change between rounds, which shows that each participant is paired with different people.
caption: Procedure for the multi-player deliberation experiment. Participants report an initial private opinion, complete three rounds of public tweet-like posts and dyadic chats with different partners, and then report a final private opinion.
abstract: Modeling opinion change through social interactions is important for understanding polarization, misinformation, and societal conflict. Recent work simulates opinion dynamics with role-playing LLM agents (RPLAs), but multi-agent simulations often display unnatural group behavior (e.g., premature convergence) and lack empirical benchmarks for assessing alignment with real human group interactions. We introduce DEBATE, a benchmark for evaluating the authenticity of opinion dynamics in multi-agent RPLA simulations. Its three-round design makes each participant's public interaction history complete and traceable. DEBATE contains multi-round public messages and private Likert-scale beliefs from U.S.-based participants across 107 topics. The dataset covers 2,788 participants in 697 groups, enabling evaluation at the utterance and group levels. We instantiate "digital twin" RPLAs with seven LLMs and evaluate across two settings: Next Message Prediction and Full Dynamics Simulation, using stance-based opinion-dynamics metrics. In zero-shot settings, RPLA groups exhibit strong opinion convergence relative to human groups. Across group-generalization tests with unseen participant groups and topic-generalization tests with unseen discussion topics, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3.5-4B, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 improves stance-based alignment and reduces excessive convergence, bringing RPLA group convergence closer to that observed in the corresponding human groups, though discrepancies in opinion change and belief updating remain. The dataset, benchmark website, and codebase are publicly available.
